sources.title: Manitoba government eyes human rights protection for gender expression - Global News (Winnipeg)
sources.claim: Global News Winnipeg (18 March 2025) reports the Manitoba NDP government plans to expand the province's Human Rights Code to cover gender expression - the code already prohibits discrimination based on gender identity, and Justice Minister Matt Wiebe says the change would bring Manitoba in line with most other provinces and cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing. The amendment sits in a government bill before the legislature, to be debated later in 2025, and is welcomed by Charlie Eau, executive director of Trans Manitoba. This is the first province-specific human-rights-protection development on record for Manitoba, filling the gap the record notes for provincial-level trans law and official statements.

sources.title: Bill to mark transgender and two-spirit day passed by Manitoba legislature - Global News (Winnipeg)
sources.claim: Global News Winnipeg (30 May 2024) reports the Manitoba legislature passed a bill recognizing March 31 as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park who is transgender. Oxenham said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported. The Legislative Assembly's passage gives Manitoba a dated, legislatively enacted trans-specific recognition at provincial level.

sources.title: Manitoba reaffirms support for trans community on Day of Remembrance - Global News (Winnipeg)
sources.claim: Global News Winnipeg (20 Nov 2023) reports Manitoba again raised the transgender flag in Winnipeg's Memorial Park for the Transgender Day of Remembrance - an observance the province first marked eight years earlier - this time with the flag raised by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. In a statement, families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara said the government 'supports and upholds the life-saving work' of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans, and Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorializes people murdered as a result of transphobia, violence she said shows no sign of slowing. This documents Manitoba's official provincial position on trans people with dates, named officials and a local advocacy voice.

records.name: England
records.current_summary:
England is where the state's law applies without a devolved layer: there is no regional administration, and the national equality institutions and courts sit principally here. The decisive recent ruling for trans visitors is the state's Supreme Court decision of 16 April 2025 settling that ‘sex’ and ‘woman’ in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological or registered sex, and that an acquired gender certificate does not change legal sex for equality-law purposes. That definition is the ground on which services, searches and detention allocation operate for anyone detained here.

How detained trans people are allocated under that definition is being actively litigated: in a June 2026 ruling applying it, a court struck down prison guidance that had allowed identity-based placement, while in the same case the state's own lawyers argued a blanket birth-sex rule would breach human rights and pose unacceptable suicide risk. Allocation practice is therefore contested and risk-laden rather than settled.

No state-specific statute, ordinance or incident series survives in this record's sources; the audit found the earlier regional assertions (administrative facility codes, transport strip-search practice, recording gaps) uncited, so England is assessed on the imposed framework alone, with no documented local deviation in either direction.

sources.claim: BBC News (19 June 2026): a judge (Lady Ross, Court of Session) ruled Scottish Prison Service guidance allowing some trans prisoners to be housed by gender identity unlawful — sex segregation in prisons must be based on biological sex, applying the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 'definition of a woman' ruling. The judgment confirms the biological-sex custody logic that the same UK-wide ruling imposes on England's prison and custody decisions; the first minister said the government will consider the judgment (the Supreme Court had already held Article 8 confers no automatic right to opposite-biological-sex accommodation).

BBC News (5 February 2026): argument of the same judicial review, in which government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy 'Orwellian'; the case tests how far the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling (cited as the predicate for England's EHRC code and BTP strip-search policy) reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide.

sources.title: Hate crime, England and Wales, year ending March 2025 - GOV.UK
sources.claim: The Home Office's England-and-Wales statistics (published 9 October 2025) record 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025, with the transgender strand down 11% and the sexual-orientation strand down 2% against the previous year; the bulletin cautions that recorded figures understate prevalence - the Crime Survey estimate is about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year - and that a February 2024 MPS recording-system change means earlier years over-counted. This gives the visitor the official England-and-Wales baseline for trans-hostile incidents in the jurisdiction where the national framework applies directly.

sources.title: Supreme Court backs 'biological' definition of woman - BBC News
sources.claim: BBC News covers the UK Supreme Court's unanimous judgment in the For Women Scotland case (handed down 16 April 2025) that 'woman' and 'sex' in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological woman and biological sex, meaning a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections; Lord Hodge said the ruling should not be read as reducing the Act's protection against discrimination for transgender people. This is the grounding source for the record's core claim - the definition that governs services, searches and detention allocation in England.

sources.title: People could be asked to prove biological sex under new EHRC code - BBC News
sources.claim: BBC News reports (20 May 2025) that the Equality and Human Rights Commission - the body enforcing the Equality Act 2010 in England and Wales - updated its code of practice after the Supreme Court ruling, advising that services and businesses may ask for a person's birth certificate where there is 'genuine concern' about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport 'when necessary' for safety. This is the operative enforcement guidance a trans visitor to England meets at venues, transport and services day to day.

records.name: Queensland
records.current_summary:
Queensland is assessed on the national framework. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised here in the 1990s reforms, and the current-status check found rights broadly advancing in line with the national standard since then.

The state's two earlier headline claims — a first-in-the-country criminal ban on conversion practices and a 2024 anti-discrimination rewrite modernising the gender-identity attribute — rest on sources that were unreachable at audit (a wire-service story behind a 401 wall; a state rights-commission page behind a 403), and one document previously cited for this region turned out to be another state's bill file. They are recorded here as unconfirmed rather than established. The state-level custody-placement divergence earlier attributed to Queensland likewise lost its citation.

What the audited record supports: no confirmed adverse state mechanism is on file either. A visitor should take the national baseline with lowered confidence in both the protective extras and any local hostility previously claimed for this state.

This is a confirmed Queensland-specific adverse health-access measure in effect for the current visit window - the kind of local mechanism the audited record said was absent.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Australia - Wikipedia (South Australia-specific provisions)
sources.claim: The page's South Australia-specific coverage records that the state was the first Australian jurisdiction to decriminalise male homosexual activity (law commenced 2 October 1975) and that it is the only jurisdiction whose scheme for historical gay convictions is 'spent' rather than expunged (Spent Convictions (Decriminalised Offences) Amendment Act 2013 in force 22 December 2013). sources.title: LGBTQ rights in South Australia - Wikipedia (dedicated article)
sources.claim: Dedicated state article recording that since 23 May 2017 (Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration (Gender Identity) Amendment Act 2016, royal assent 15 December 2016) a South Australian can change the sex descriptor on a birth certificate with appropriate clinical treatment, with no sex-reassignment surgery or forced divorce if married; non-binary and 'indeterminate' sex descriptors are also available on state birth certificates. It records the hate-crime sentencing laws explicitly including sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics, passed and implemented November 2021; the gay-panic defence abolished on 1 December 2020 and effective 1 April 2021; and the Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2024, passed October 2024 and in legal effect 1 April 2025. It also records that the state's Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2016 to protect gender identity and sexual orientation, that same-sex couples could adopt from 17 February 2017, and that same-sex marriage has been legal since December 2017 (the 2017 postal survey returning 62.5% 'Yes' in South Australia). For this record: the state-level statute and enforcement facts (especially the birth-certificate marker regime and hate-crime sentencing) that the current summary says are undocumented for South Australia.

The one operational divergence earlier claimed for this state — prisoners placed on an explicit self-identification basis, shared with only a handful of the country's jurisdictions — lost its documentary support at audit: the file previously cited for it belongs to a different state, and the surviving sources for Tasmania were unreachable at fetch time (a 401-walled wire story and a 403-blocked commission page, both describing national developments). sources.title: LGBT rights in Australia – Wikipedia
sources.claim: The article dates Tasmania's equality timeline precisely: after the Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994, Tasmania still refused to repeal its anti-gay Criminal Code provisions and, faced with a likely High Court loss in Croome v Tasmania, decriminalised male homosexuality with effect from 14 May 1997 — the final Australian jurisdiction to do so. It records that the age of consent in Tasmania is 17 (one of only two jurisdictions with South Australia), that same-sex couples can enter into domestic registered partnerships in Tasmania with an optional official ceremony, that equality of adoption rights for same-sex couples applied in all states and territories from April 2018, and that as of 2019 Tasmania issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates. Corroborates this record's account that Tasmania reached formal legal equality via the national framework with no state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern documented, while flagging the one standing statutory particularity — the 17 age of consent — not covered by the record's summary.

sources.title: Tasmania makes gender optional on birth certificates after Liberal crosses floor – ABC News
sources.claim: ABC News reported on 11 April 2019 that Tasmania's House of Assembly passed the Marriage Amendments Bill the previous day (10 April 2019) after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition, the legislation having already passed the Legislative Council. The reforms make gender on birth certificates optional, remove the requirement that transgender people undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised, and let people aged 16 or older change their registered gender without parental approval, with the Tasmanian Government having opposed the amendments and declining to rule out later repeal. State-specific enactment-level evidence for the equal-status finding in this record: the operational reform a trans visitor to Tasmania stands under, passed against government resistance rather than reflecting any criminalisation or incident series.
